plants.title: Plants

tomato.name: Tomato
tomato.description: Warm-season crop, needs staking. Very productive in good conditions.

zucchini.name: Zucchini
zucchini.description: Prolific summer squash. One or two plants are usually enough.

carrot.name: Carrot
carrot.description: Root vegetable that prefers loose, sandy soil. Direct sow only.

lettuce.name: Lettuce
lettuce.description: Fast-growing salad green. Prefers cooler temperatures.

bean.name: Bush Bean
bean.description: Nitrogen-fixing legume. Easy to grow, productive.

pea.name: Pea
pea.description: Cool-season crop. Sow early in spring, harvest before heat.

radish.name: Radish
radish.description: Very fast-growing root vegetable. Ready in 25–30 days.

cucumber.name: Cucumber
cucumber.description: Needs warmth and consistent watering. Great for trellising.

pepper.name: Bell Pepper
pepper.description: Heat-loving plant. Start indoors early for best results.

onion.name: Onion
onion.description: Long-season crop. Start from sets or transplants for best results.

garlic.name: Garlic
garlic.description: Plant in autumn, harvest next summer. Very low maintenance.

potato.name: Potato
potato.description: Staple crop. Needs hilling as it grows. Good for beginners.

strawberry.name: Strawberry
strawberry.description: Perennial berry. Produces fruit for several years.

raspberry.name: Raspberry
raspberry.description: Perennial berry bush. Needs a trellis or support.

blueberry.name: Blueberry
blueberry.description: Needs acidic soil. Produces fruit after 2–3 years.

basil.name: Basil
basil.description: Annual herb, great companion for tomatoes. Loves warmth.

parsley.name: Parsley
parsley.description: Biennial herb. Slow to germinate but very versatile.

dill.name: Dill
dill.description: Annual herb. Attracts beneficial insects. Self-seeds readily.

chives.name: Chives
chives.description: Perennial herb with mild onion flavor. Very easy to grow.

kale.name: Kale
kale.description: Hardy leafy green. Tastes sweeter after frost.

spinach.name: Spinach
spinach.description: Cool-season green. Bolts quickly in heat.

beetroot.name: Beetroot
beetroot.description: Dual-purpose: eat both roots and leaves. Easy to grow.

leek.name: Leek
leek.description: Hardy allium. Needs blanching for white stems.

pumpkin.name: Pumpkin
pumpkin.description: Needs lots of space. Great for storage over winter.

chard.name: Swiss Chard
chard.description: Colorful, productive green. Harvest outer leaves for continuous yield.

kohlrabi.name: Kohlrabi
kohlrabi.description: Fast-growing brassica. Eat the swollen stem raw or cooked.

fennel.name: Fennel
fennel.description: Anise-flavored bulb vegetable. Does not grow well near most other plants.

corn.name: Corn
corn.description: Tall-growing cereal. Plant in blocks for good pollination.

sunflower.name: Sunflower
sunflower.description: Attracts pollinators. Edible seeds and great for companion planting.

cabbage.name: Cabbage
cabbage.description: Cool-season brassica. Good for sauerkraut and storage.

broccoli.name: Broccoli
broccoli.description: Harvest the main head, then side shoots keep producing.

cauliflower.name: Cauliflower
cauliflower.description: Needs consistent conditions. Blanch heads by tying leaves.

celery.name: Celery
celery.description: Long-season crop that needs rich soil and consistent moisture.

turnip.name: Turnip
turnip.description: Quick-growing root vegetable. Both roots and greens are edible.

mint.name: Mint
mint.description: Vigorous perennial herb. Best grown in containers to prevent spreading.

rosemary.name: Rosemary
rosemary.description: Woody perennial herb. Drought-tolerant once established.

thyme.name: Thyme
thyme.description: Low-growing perennial herb. Excellent ground cover.

currant.name: Currant
currant.description: Hardy berry bush. Red and black varieties available.

gooseberry.name: Gooseberry
gooseberry.description: Thorny berry bush. Excellent for jams and desserts.

eggplant.name: Eggplant
eggplant.description: Heat-loving solanaceous fruit. Needs warm conditions and rich soil.

arugula.name: Arugula
arugula.description: Peppery salad green. Fast-growing cool-season crop, ready in weeks.

squash.name: Butternut Squash
squash.description: Winter squash with sweet, nutty flesh. Stores well for months.

asparagus.name: Asparagus
asparagus.description: Perennial vegetable. Takes 2–3 years to establish but produces for 15+ years.

pak_choi.name: Pak Choi
pak_choi.description: Fast-growing Asian green with crisp white stems and tender leaves.

endive.name: Endive
endive.description: Slightly bitter salad green. Blanch hearts for milder flavor.

lambs_lettuce.name: Lamb's lettuce
lambs_lettuce.description: Hardy winter salad. Sow from July to early October, harvest from autumn to spring.

winter_purslane.name: Winter purslane
winter_purslane.description: Hardy salad green with succulent leaves. Sow in August and September, under glass until the end of October; harvest into spring.

pantry.tip1: Always label jars and freezer bags with the date and contents.
pantry.tip2: Store canned goods in a cool, dark, dry place. Avoid direct sunlight.
pantry.tip3: Blanch vegetables before freezing for better color, texture and nutrient retention.
pantry.tip4: Check fermented foods regularly — remove any surface mold immediately.
pantry.tip5: Root cellar storage needs 1–4 °C and high humidity. Keep potatoes in the dark.
pantry.tip6: Use the “first in, first out” principle – eat the oldest preserves first.

canning.desc: Preserve fruits, vegetables and sauces in jars. Water bath for acidic foods, pressure canner for vegetables.

freezing.desc: Quick freezing preserves nutrients and flavor. Blanch vegetables first. Pack airtight.

fermenting.desc: Lacto-fermentation preserves and creates probiotics. Salt, water and time — no heat needed.

drying.desc: Dehydrator or oven at low temperature. Ideal for herbs, tomatoes, apples, mushrooms.

root_cellar.desc: Cool, humid storage for root vegetables, potatoes, apples, cabbage. 1–4 °C optimal.

health.subtitle: Vaccinations, treatments and check-ups at a glance.
health.dueHow: Poultry, rabbits, goats and sheep without a vaccination in the last {{days}} days. Bees are not vaccinated. Intervals depend on the vaccine and your vet.

vaccContext.chicken: Chickens: in Germany vaccination against Newcastle disease (ND) is mandatory. The interval depends on the vaccine – hatchery chicks are often already vaccinated against Marek’s disease.
vaccContext.poultry: Ducks and quail: not mandatory, but ND vaccination is recommended. The interval depends on the vaccine.
vaccContext.rabbit: Rabbits: RHD and myxomatosis, every six to twelve months depending on the vaccine.
vaccContext.ruminant: Goats and sheep: clostridial vaccine, usually boosted yearly – check with your vet.
vaccContext.other: The interval depends on the vaccine – check with your vet.

soil.title: Soil
soil.subtitle: Interpret soil tests and record amendments per bed.
soil.emptyTestsText: A simple pH and nutrient test per bed tells you whether to lime, feed or simply wait.
soil.emptyAmendmentsText: Record what you applied and when – compost, manure, lime. That way you avoid over-fertilising.
soil.targetHint: Target range for the crops in this bed: pH {{range}}

phAdvice.limeStrong: Well below the target range (pH {{range}}). Apply garden lime or calcified seaweed, ideally in autumn, and test again after a year.
phAdvice.limeLight: Slightly below the target range (pH {{range}}). A small dose of calcified seaweed is enough – do not over-lime.
phAdvice.optimal: Within the crops' target range (pH {{range}}). No lime or sulphur needed – nothing to do for the pH.
phAdvice.noLime: Slightly above the target range (pH {{range}}). Do not lime and no wood ash. Leaf mould, bark compost and pine needles lower the pH slowly; ordinary garden compost is neutral to alkaline, so use it sparingly. Sulphur is not needed.
phAdvice.sulfur: Well above the target range (pH {{range}}). Work in elemental sulphur in small doses; no lime and no wood ash.
phAdvice.limeVeto: Do not lime: pH {{ph}} suits {{crops}} (target {{range}}). {{reason}} The other crops in the bed cope with it; lime after the harvest, for the next crop.
phAdvice.averseHigh: Slightly too high for {{crops}} (target {{range}}). {{reason}} Do not lime, no wood ash; leaf mould or bark compost lowers the pH slowly.
phAdvice.acidify: Far too high for {{crops}} (target {{range}}). Fill the bed or planting hole with acidic substrate (ericaceous compost, composted bark) or lower the pH slowly with elemental sulphur. Water with rainwater; tap water is often hard.

soil.ppmHint: Nutrients in ppm (mg/kg), as test kits and labs report them. Leave fields empty if not measured.

limeReason.blueberry: Blueberries need acidic soil and do not tolerate lime.
limeReason.raspberry: Raspberries react to lime with yellow leaves (chlorosis).

soil.brassicaNote: Brassicas benefit twice: a pH around 7 also helps prevent clubroot.

nitrogen.low: Nitrogen low: give compost or hoof and horn meal (50–100 g/m²) before hungry crops; sow legumes as green manure in autumn.
nitrogen.high: Nitrogen high: hold off nitrogen feeds, grow light feeders or green manure – too much nitrogen makes leafy greens high in nitrate.

phosphorus.low: Phosphorus low: work in well-rotted manure or compost.
phosphorus.high: Phosphorus high, common in home gardens: no manure, little compost and no phosphate-containing general fertiliser; add nitrogen only, with hoof and horn meal.

potassium.low: Potassium low: comfrey tea, sulphate of potash or a little wood ash (not at high pH).
potassium.high: Potassium high: no potassium fertiliser and no wood ash.

organicMatter.low: Organic matter low: mulch, sow green manure and add 2–3 l of compost per m² every year.
organicMatter.high: Organic matter very high: cut back on compost for a few years.

metrics.recordedSince: Harvests and animal products since 1 January {{year}}
metrics.howForecast: Annual forecast: planted area × expected yield per m² of each crop, plus the typical annual yield of your animals (e.g. 220 eggs per hen, 20 kg honey per colony).
metrics.howActual: Recorded so far: your harvest entries and animal products since 1 January, by the same rule. Entries without a weight are not counted.
metrics.howNeed: Self-sufficiency = the share of your household's calorie need ({{kcal}} kcal per person per day) that garden and animals cover in a year (at most 100%).
metrics.pricesEditable: You can adjust the price per egg, kg or litre on the Costs page.
metrics.howCap: Animal products count only up to typical consumption (per person and year about 240 eggs, 1 kg honey, 52 kg meat, 300 l milk). Honey is calorie-dense but not a staple: two colonies give about 40 kg, a household eats 1–2 kg of it. Anything above is surplus to swap or sell and does not feed you. Vegetables and fruit count in full.
metrics.howToDate: Expected by today: the part of the annual forecast that should be in by now – each crop's harvest window from the last frost, honey May to August, eggs evenly over the year. If “recorded so far” is well below it, entries are usually missing.
metrics.howVsFoodPlan: The food plan measures something else: kilograms against a quantity target for 20 vegetable and fruit crops, without animal products. Its “quantity target” therefore differs from this calorie figure.
metrics.compositionTitle: What the forecast is made of
metrics.compositionDesc: Share of the annual calorie need, by source.
metrics.compositionLabel: Garden {{garden}}, animal products {{animals}} of the annual need
